title: Hammurabi and the Amorite Kingdoms
subtitle: 2004–1595 BC · Isin and Larsa, Shamshi-Adad and Mari, the Law Stele, and the Fall of the First Dynasty of Babylon

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The successor kingdoms of Isin and Larsa, Shamshi-Adad's northern realm and the Mari of Zimri-Lim, and the thirty patient years and swift conquest of Hammurabi of Babylon

entries.label: Isin inherits the kingship of Ur
entries.hint: Ishbi-Erra, the officer who had broken away from Ibbi-Sin, founded a dynasty at Isin that held Nippur and claimed to have taken up the fallen kingship of Ur. Its kings kept the Sumerian royal-hymn tradition alive, issued a law collection under Lipit-Ishtar, and dominated the south for a century — until Larsa overtook them and Rim-Sin captured the city in 1794.
entries.note: Douglas Frayne, RIME 4: 'Old Babylonian Period' (1990); Dietz Otto Edzard, 'Die "zweite Zwischenzeit" Babyloniens' (1957).

entries.label: Larsa takes the lead in the south
entries.hint: Under Gungunum, Larsa wrested Ur from Isin in 1927 and campaigned into Elam, and over the next century it displaced Isin as the strongest southern kingdom. Larsa's wealth came from the date gardens and wool of the deep south and from the sun-god Shamash's great temple, the Ebabbar, whose archives document the shift of the region's centre of gravity away from Nippur.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); the Larsa economy in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'Society and Enterprise in Old Babylonian Ur' (1992).

entries.label: Kudur-Mabuk's line and the long reign of Rim-Sin
entries.hint: The Elamite chief Kudur-Mabuk set his sons over Larsa — first Warad-Sin, then Rim-Sin I, who reigned some sixty years. Rim-Sin conquered Isin in 1794 and was so proud of it that he dated his regnal years by that conquest for the next thirty. He ruled the whole south from the Gulf to Nippur, and was one of the two most powerful kings in the land, until Hammurabi defeated and deposed him in 1763.
entries.note: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'The Reign of Rim-Sin' (RA 1993); Frayne, RIME 4 (1990).

entries.label: Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia
entries.hint: An Amorite from the Ekallatum line, Shamshi-Adad seized Assur, then Mari, then the whole northern Jazira, and ruled it from a rebuilt capital, Shubat-Enlil, delegating Ekallatum to his capable son Ishme-Dagan and Mari to his idle son Yasmah-Addu. It was the first territorial state to unite the north — and it broke apart within a year of his death.
entries.note: Dominique Charpin & Nele Ziegler, 'Mari et le Proche-Orient à l'époque amorrite' (2003); the Shamshi-Adad correspondence in the Mari archives.

entries.label: Zimri-Lim of Mari and the great palace
entries.hint: After Shamshi-Adad's death the old Lim dynasty returned to Mari in the person of Zimri-Lim, who held the middle Euphrates, married a daughter of Yarim-Lim of Aleppo, and kept a court whose sprawling palace and archive of more than twenty thousand letters and records is the richest window we have on the age. His ally Hammurabi captured Mari in 1761 and levelled it two years later.
entries.note: Jean-Marie Durand, 'Les documents épistolaires du palais de Mari' I–III (1997–2000); Wolfgang Heimpel, 'Letters to the King of Mari' (2003).

entries.label: The merchant city-state of Assur
entries.hint: Except for the interval under Shamshi-Adad, Assur was a small oligarchic city-state on the Tigris governed jointly by a hereditary 'steward', an official who gave his name to the year, and an assembly known simply as 'the City'. It had little land and no army worth the name; its entire wealth came from running the caravan trade to Anatolia.
entries.note: Klaas Veenhof & Jesper Eidem, 'Mesopotamia: The Old Assyrian Period' (OBO 160/5, 2008); Mogens Trolle Larsen, 'The Old Assyrian City-State and its Colonies' (1976).

entries.label: The First Dynasty builds Babylon
entries.hint: Five Amorite kings from Sumu-abum to Sin-muballit turned Babylon from an obscure town into a middling kingdom of northern Babylonia — Sippar, Kish, Borsippa, Dilbat — walling the city, digging canals, and fighting Larsa, Isin and Eshnunna for room. It was a modest inheritance, and it is the base from which Hammurabi built an empire.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Marc Van De Mieroop, 'King Hammurabi of Babylon: A Biography' (2005), ch. 1.

entries.label: Hammurabi of Babylon
entries.hint: For most of his forty-three years Hammurabi was one strong king among several — a Mari report ranks him level with Rim-Sin of Larsa and Ibal-pi-El of Eshnunna, each with ten or fifteen lesser kings 'following' him. Then from 1764 he moved fast: he broke an Elamite-led coalition, took Larsa, crushed Eshnunna, destroyed his ally Mari, and subdued Assyria, ruling all Mesopotamia by 1755. His year-names and his law stele record it.
entries.note: Marc Van De Mieroop, 'King Hammurabi of Babylon' (2005); Dominique Charpin, 'Hammurabi of Babylon' (2012); the 'ten kings' letter is Mari text ARM VI 27.

entries.label: Samsu-iluna and the loss of the south
entries.hint: Hammurabi's son inherited the empire and immediately faced a vast revolt — a pretender styling himself Rim-Sin II, joined by Eshnunna, the southern cities and the Kassites. He held the north but lost the south for good: Ur, Uruk, Larsa and Nippur were abandoned around 1740, their archives falling silent, and a 'Sealand' dynasty took the marshes. Babylon contracted to its home region.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Seth Richardson, 'The Collapse of a Complex State: A Reappraisal of the End of the First Dynasty of Babylon' (2002).

entries.label: The late kings and the Venus tablet
entries.hint: Abi-eshuh, Ammi-ditana, Ammi-saduqa and their successors ruled a shrunken kingdom of northern Babylonia — consolidating, digging canals, repeatedly cancelling debts by decree, and absorbing Kassite groups as soldiers and workers. Ammi-saduqa's reign produced the tablet of Venus observations that anchors the whole disputed chronology of the Bronze Age.
entries.note: Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Erica Reiner & David Pingree, 'The Venus Tablet of Ammiṣaduqa' (1975).

entries.label: Samsu-ditana and the Hittite sack
entries.hint: The last king of the dynasty ruled thirty years over the diminished kingdom, and then, around 1595, the Hittite king Mursili I struck down the Euphrates in a raid of unheard-of range, sacked Babylon, and carried off the statues of Marduk and his consort. The dynasty ended. After a murky interval, the Kassites — long resident in the land — took the throne.
entries.note: The Hittite 'Edict of Telipinu' and the 'Chronicle of Early Kings'; Trevor Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

entries.label: The kings who called each other brother
entries.hint: The Mari letters show an international system: a dozen Amorite kingdoms from the Zagros to the Mediterranean whose rulers addressed one another as 'brother' among equals or 'father' and 'son' by rank, sent resident envoys, sealed treaties by touching the throat and swearing by the gods, married across borders, and shared pastoral tribes whose loyalties crossed every frontier. It is the earliest well-documented diplomacy of the ancient world.
entries.note: Jean-Marie Durand, 'La diplomatie mésopotamienne'; Bertrand Lafont, 'Relations internationales, alliances et diplomatie au temps des rois de Mari' (2001).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Isin–Larsa rivalry and the wars of the 'ten kings', Hammurabi's campaigns of unification, the destruction of Mari, the great revolt and the loss of the south, and the Hittite raid that ended the dynasty

entries.label: Isin against Larsa
entries.hint: For well over a century Isin and Larsa fought a war of attrition over the south — for Ur, for the sun-temple at Larsa, and above all for control of Nippur, whose god Enlil conferred legitimate kingship over the land. Nippur changed hands repeatedly, kings dated their years by its capture, and the contest ended only when Rim-Sin of Larsa took Isin itself in 1794.
entries.note: Reconstructed from year-names and inscriptions in Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); D. O. Edzard (1957).

entries.group: The Wars of the Ten Kings
entries.label: The shifting coalitions of the 1770s
entries.loc: the middle Euphrates and the plain
entries.hint: The Mari archive captures a decade of fluid, multi-sided war: Babylon, Larsa, Eshnunna, Elam as would-be overlord, Mari, Aleppo, Qatna and the mountain Turukkeans forming and breaking alliances season by season. One much-quoted report tells the king of Mari that no ruler is strong alone — 'ten or fifteen kings follow Hammurabi, as many follow Rim-Sin, as many Ibal-pi-El of Eshnunna.'
entries.note: Mari text ARM VI 27 and the wider correspondence; Wolfgang Heimpel, 'Letters to the King of Mari' (2003).

entries.label: The conquest of Mesopotamia, 1764–1755
entries.hint: In his thirtieth year Hammurabi shattered a coalition led by Elam; in his thirty-first he conquered Rim-Sin's Larsa and the whole south; in his thirty-second he beat Eshnunna, the Gutians and Subartu; then he took Mari, and finally reduced Assyria. In little more than a decade a mid-sized kingdom became the master of Mesopotamia — a transformation his own year-names narrate step by step.
entries.note: Hammurabi's year-names 30–38 in Frayne, RIME 4 (1990); Charpin, 'Hammurabi of Babylon' (2012).

entries.label: The destruction of Mari
entries.hint: Hammurabi took Mari from his former ally Zimri-Lim in 1761, garrisoned it, and two years later pulled down its walls and set fire to the great palace. The fire baked and buried the twenty-thousand-tablet archive where it lay. Mari's ruin was a strategic act; its unintended result was to preserve the fullest record of Amorite Mesopotamia for the excavators of the 1930s.
entries.note: André Parrot's Mari excavations; the destruction in Charpin & Ziegler (2003) and Durand's archive editions.

entries.label: The great revolt and the abandonment of Sumer
entries.hint: A coalition rising in Samsu-iluna's tenth year — a pretender, Eshnunna, the southern cities and the Kassites — was beaten in the north but won in the south. Within a decade the old Sumerian cities were emptying: temple archives break off, canals silted, the population drained toward the north or into the marshes, where a 'Sealand' dynasty held out. The heartland of Sumer, urban for two thousand years, was largely abandoned for the next several centuries.
entries.note: Seth Richardson, 'The Collapse of a Complex State' (2002); the settlement evidence in Robert McC. Adams, 'Heartland of Cities' (1981).

entries.group: The Fall of the First Dynasty
entries.label: The Hittite raid on Babylon
entries.hint: The Hittite king Mursili I, having destroyed Aleppo, drove on down the Euphrates in a strike of unprecedented reach, took Babylon, plundered it, and carried the statues of Marduk and Sarpanitu back toward Anatolia (they were later recovered from Hana). He did not stay — but the First Dynasty was finished, and after a gap of uncertain length the Kassites ruled Babylon.
entries.note: The Hittite 'Edict of Telipinu' and the Babylonian 'Chronicle of Early Kings'; Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).
